Let’s talk about something we don’t always notice— the subtle courage of vulnerability.
You know, we often think of courage as this big, heroic moment—charging into danger, making a bold stand, or doing something that gets everyone’s attention.
But there’s another kind of courage that’s a lot quieter, and honestly, just as powerful. It’s the courage to let yourself be vulnerable. To admit you’re scared. To ask for help, even when it’s tough. To keep moving forward, step by shaky step, when you’re not sure you’re enough.
That’s the kind of courage Piglet lives out, day after day.
Think about someone—maybe it’s even you—who feels anxious about speaking up in a group. That worry about saying the wrong thing, or being misunderstood, is so real. Yet, when a friend is going through something tough, somehow you find the words, even if your voice is barely above a whisper.
You reach out, not because you’re fearless, but because you care more about helping than about how uncomfortable you feel. That is what real courage looks like—showing up, even when it’s hard.
Piglet’s vulnerability is right there in every story. He’s honest about his fears. He never tries to act braver than he really is. When a storm rolls in or the woods feel dark, Piglet doesn’t pretend he’s not scared—he lets his friends see him tremble.
But here’s the thing: he still moves forward. Not because he’s fearless, but because his friends need him. There’s this beautiful moment when Piglet faces something that feels huge and he says, “I’m not very brave, but I’ll try.”
That promise means more than a thousand boasts.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength it takes to be honest about what scares you. We’re taught to hide our weaknesses, to keep up a tough front. But when someone’s willing to be vulnerable, it gives everyone around them permission to drop their guard, too. That’s when real connection happens—when we stop pretending and just show up as ourselves.
Sometimes, Piglet’s friends overlook his quiet courage. They see his smallness, his gentle voice, and they think he’s timid. But when things get tough, it’s Piglet who steps forward—not because he’s unafraid, but because he chooses to act, even with fear tagging along.
That’s the heart of true bravery.
Piglet shows us that vulnerability isn’t something to hide away—it’s actually a doorway. It leads to deeper friendships, to trust, and to real growth. When you let yourself be seen—scared, unsure, but still willing—you inspire others to do the same.
The world doesn’t need more bravado. It needs more people who are willing to be real.
